regime.justification: Asian equities sold off sharply overnight on a semiconductor-led unwind of AI-trade valuations that started in US chip stocks and spilled into the region — Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.6% to below 67,000 (the broader Topix dropped 0.8% to 4,055), snapping a two-day winning streak as AI-linked equipment makers including Advantest, SoftBank Group, and Tokyo Electron sold off hard; South Korea's KOSPI plunged more than 7% and the small-cap Kosdaq fell 5% in the same rout. Against that, Australia's ASX 200 held up relatively well (+0.23% to 8,829.20, likely cushioned by resource and oil-linked names), Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 1.70% to 24,755.56, and mainland China's Shanghai Composite eased 0.22% to 3,958.59 — a genuinely mixed regional picture rather than a uniform flight from risk. Separately, and on its own track, the Iran/Strait of Hormuz crisis (United States vs. Iran) widened further: the Strait is now effectively closed to commercial shipping (only around 10 vessels transited versus a normal ~88 per day), the US military completed a second wave of strikes on Iran Wednesday aimed at degrading its ability to target vessels in the Strait, Washington has reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and roughly 6,000 seafarers remain stranded aboard stranded vessels across the Gulf. Brent crude extended its rally for a fourth consecutive session (~$85.90, versus Wednesday's $84.73 close) to fresh crisis highs, while gold held broadly steady in the $4,060-4,070/oz area — still not showing the sharp safe-haven bid the scale of the crisis might otherwise imply, a continuation of the paradox this report has flagged repeatedly. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Senate Banking Committee testimony as chair (US Federal Reserve, United States) took place Wednesday: he reaffirmed the Fed's anti-inflation commitment ("no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation") but, per multiple outlets, gave few fresh clues on the actual rate path, faced sharp ethics-focused questioning from Senator Elizabeth Warren, and confirmed regular (if undetailed) contact with the Trump administration. The Bank of Canada (Canada) delivered the fully-priced outcome — a sixth consecutive hold at 2.25%, with a fresh Monetary Policy Report flagging the Middle East war and US trade policy as the key risks to the outlook, and May CPI at 3.2% (gasoline-driven).
regime.executiveSummary: Today is genuinely two shocks running in parallel rather than one clean narrative. The first is a specific, contained equity story: an AI-valuation reassessment hitting semiconductor and AI-infrastructure names hardest, which is why Japan and Korea are down sharply while Australia, Hong Kong, and mainland China are comparatively unbothered — this is a sector rotation, not (yet) a broad risk-off wave. The second is the Iran/Hormuz war continuing to escalate on its own track — the Strait effectively shut, a US naval blockade reimposed, two waves of US strikes this week — with oil the clearest transmission channel (a fourth straight day of gains) while broader risk sentiment outside the semiconductor complex has so far shrugged it off, echoing the "commodity story, not a risk-off trigger" pattern flagged in this report for over a week. Layered on top, Fed Chair Warsh's Senate testimony was a non-event for the market-pricing-versus-rhetoric tension flagged yesterday: he neither confirmed the market's dovish lean (sub-17% odds of a September hike, per prior sessions) nor delivered fresh hawkish conviction, leaving that gap exactly where it was. The Bank of Canada's hold carried no surprise. Today's still-pending US data (Retail Sales, Initial Jobless Claims, Philadelphia Fed) are this session's next concrete catalysts, alongside a genuinely urgent internal issue for this report: a severe same-session data conflict on AUD/NZD — this tracker's highest-conviction open idea — that is significant enough to be flagged prominently rather than resolved by picking a source (see Section 2).

**Executive Summary:** Today is genuinely two shocks running in parallel rather than one clean narrative. The first is a specific, contained equity story: an AI-valuation reassessment hitting semiconductor and AI-infrastructure names hardest, which is why Japan and Korea are down sharply while Australia, Hong Kong, and mainland China are comparatively unbothered — this is a sector rotation, not (yet) a broad risk-off wave. The second is the Iran/Hormuz war continuing to escalate on its own track — the Strait effectively shut, a US naval blockade reimposed, two waves of US strikes this week — with oil the clearest transmission channel (a fourth straight day of gains) while broader risk sentiment outside the semiconductor complex has so far shrugged it off, echoing the "commodity story, not a risk-off trigger" pattern flagged in this report for over a week. Layered on top, Fed Chair Warsh's Senate testimony was a non-event for the market-pricing-versus-rhetoric tension flagged yesterday: he neither confirmed the market's dovish lean (sub-17% odds of a September hike, per prior sessions) nor delivered fresh hawkish conviction, leaving that gap exactly where it was.
